---
title: "Stage 0 — map the protocol to ICH M11"
---

Establishing what the protocol says, against a fixed list of what a protocol is supposed to
contain — and where it says it.

## What this is

ICH M11 is a template for the clinical trial protocol. It has fourteen sections and, in the
merged electronic version, 303 data elements, 216 of them required and nearly all carrying a
CDISC code. Those counts belong to one release, v0.17.0 of the electronic specification, which
is what this book was mapped against; the next release will move them.

**Where you start depends on where the protocol came from, and the two cases are different
pieces of work.**

*If the protocol was authored to M11* — the case M11 exists for — the structure is already
there. This stage is a **confirmation**: which elements does the endpoint you are carrying
depend on, and does the protocol actually supply them? Authoring to a template does not
guarantee completeness, and a section can be present and empty. Expect this to take an hour,
not a week.

*If the protocol predates M11, or was written to a sponsor's own template* — the common case
today, and the one this book walks — it is a **mapping**: deciding, element by element, which
piece of the existing document answers it, and recording the ones nothing answers.

The two produce different things. Confirmation produces a checklist. Mapping produces a
diagnosis, because the elements nothing answers tell you something about the document that no
amount of reading it end to end will.

This book takes the mapping path because the study it uses predates M11. If you are starting a
new protocol, read this stage for what the elements *are* and then skip to the confirmation
version of the steps below.

## What you do

**Mapping an existing protocol**

1. List the M11 elements the endpoint you are carrying depends on. Not all 216; only the ones
   in scope.
2. For each, find where the existing document answers it, and write down the location.
3. Where nothing answers it, record *absent*, and where you believe the content lives instead.
4. Produce a table, not an edit. The output of this stage is a description of the document as it
   stands.

**Confirming a protocol authored to M11**

1. List the same in-scope elements.
2. Check each is present *and populated* — a heading with nothing under it satisfies a template
   and not a reader.
3. Record the gaps. There will be fewer, and they will be genuine omissions rather than
   misplacements.

Either way, the absences are the interesting half, so record them with the same care as the
matches.

## What you should see

A mapping document, and a count of required elements the protocol does not supply.

On a protocol not written to M11, expect that count to be substantial: it measures the distance
between two conventions, not how good the protocol is. On one authored to M11 it should be
close to zero, and anything that is not zero is worth understanding before you go further.

### Step into the factory

The mapping this book was written from is `study/m11/protocol-to-m11.md`: element by element,
for the sections the two endpoints depend on, with the location in the source protocol or the
word *absent* against each. Where the element counts above came from, and the command that
reproduces them, is the ICH M11 entry in `study/source-refs.md`.

## What to look out for

**Most of what looks missing is misplaced.** The commonest case is the estimand. M11 §3.1.1
wants it *in the protocol*, and five of that section's seven required elements are ICH E9(R1)
estimand attributes, but the long-standing convention is to define estimands in the
statistical analysis plan. A protocol written that way fails a stack of required elements while
the study itself is perfectly well specified. Record such an element as *absent here, held in that document*
rather than as missing, or the mapping reads as an indictment when it is a translation.

**Resist fixing anything at this stage.** The urge to correct the protocol while mapping it is
strong, and it destroys the measurement: once you have edited, you can no longer say what the
protocol did say, and the count becomes a count of your own edits.

**Expect the same element in several places, disagreeing.** A synopsis, a body section and an
appendix will each carry a version of the population, or the randomisation ratio, and they will
not always agree. Which one is authoritative is a decision, and it should be a recorded one.

**Map the whole of a section, not the part that feeds your endpoint.** Reading selectively
means the first thing you learn about the rest is that it does not fit, usually much later.
